title: Act II, Scene I

teacherSummary.text: Alone in his orchard at night, Brutus decides Caesar must die, not for what he has done but for what he might become: 'think him as a serpent's egg.' He reads a forged letter urging him to act. The conspirators arrive; Brutus refuses an oath, refuses to include Cicero, and overrules Cassius's plan to kill Antony too: 'Let us be sacrificers, but not butchers.' Decius promises to bring Caesar to the Capitol. Portia, who has wounded her own thigh to prove her constancy, demands to share his secret. Ligarius, though sick, joins.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act II, Scene I,” how does Shakespeare show Brutus decides? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act II, Scene I, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of Brutus decides? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act II, Scene I develops the idea of Brutus decides. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act II, Scene I (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of Brutus decides. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act II, Scene I suggests about Brutus decides. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's characterization and theme), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses characterization in Act II, Scene I to complicate the reader's understanding of Brutus decides. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act II, Scene I within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of Brutus decides responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act II, Scene I alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of Brutus decides follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act II, Scene I and its treatment of Brutus decides. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's characterization and theme, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act II, Scene I as evidence for a larger claim about Brutus decides in Julius Caesar. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act II, Scene I as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of Brutus decides. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Julius Caesar.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Is it fair to punish someone for something they might do in the future? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script:
Today's words are husbanded, dismember, unbraced, appertain, discard. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “Think you I am no stronger than my sex,
Being so father’d and so husbanded?” In this sentence it means: married; having a husband. Word histories: “discard”: dis- "away" + card (playing card): originally "to throw a card out of one's hand," then "to cast off." For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Julius Caesar would have known. Brutus's ancestor, Lucius Junius Brutus, was said to have driven out Rome's last king, Tarquin, and founded the republic. That family history weighs on Brutus. Why does this scene matter? Brutus's soliloquy argues from fear of the future, not evidence. His three decisions here (no oath, no Cicero, spare Antony) each show idealism and each later harms the conspiracy. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “Let ’em enter.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to Brutus decides? I circle “prevention”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find characterization, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for characterization.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this scene connect to power, ambition and tyranny? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes Brutus decides. Tonight, read the next scene and add two words to your etymology log.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
